71	
72	### 5.1 Instructions (rules)
73	
74	The complete rules (adapted from earlier tests of this approach):
75	
76	- One printer fits: call the tool with it.
77	- Two or three genuinely fit: call the tool with all of them, and ask in your reply what tells them apart.
78	- More than three fit: do not call the tool. Ask one question that narrows it down and say where to look, or point to "Browse the list". Never show three of many.
79	- A query that is the start of more than one model name is not a clear match, even when it exactly equals one of them.
80	- Nothing fits, or it isn't a filament printer: say so in one sentence; do not call the tool.
81	- A photo: name a model only from a readable name or a printed size. Going by shape alone, ask for a photo of the label (a sticker on the back, a plate under the frame, the About page on the screen). Never quote a label as read unless asking the person to confirm it. Never judge size from how big it looks. A clone uses the profile of the model it copies.
82	- Write every reply from the facts the tool returns, never from memory.
83	
84	### 5.2 Description (verbatim)
85	
86	> You decide which printer this is. This tool checks the printers you name against the app's printer list, shows them to the person, and returns the details to mention. It never picks a printer.
87	
88	### 5.3 Input
89	
90	```json
91	{ "catalogIds": ["Prusa/MK3S"],   // 1 to 3, copied exactly from the printer list
92	  "nozzle": 0.6 }                  // optional, mm; only when the person or a photo said so
93	```
94	
95	Nothing else. The count carries the model's certainty: one id means sure, and the card offers "Add this printer"; two or three mean unsure, and each card offers "This one".
96	
97	### 5.4 Output (JSON)
98	
99	```json
100	{ "printers": [
101	    { "catalogId": "Prusa/MK3S",
102	      "brand": "Prusa",
103	      "model": "MK3S",
104	      "buildVolume": "250 × 210 × 210 mm",
105	      "nozzles": [0.25, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8],
106	      "assumed": { "nozzle": 0.4, "plate": null, "filament": "Prusa Generic PLA" },
107	      "alreadyYours": false } ] }
108	```
109	
110	| Field | Where the app gets it |
111	| --- | --- |
112	| `brand` | `resources/profiles/<Vendor>.json`, its `name` |
113	| `model` | The model's profile name with the brand not repeated |
114	| `buildVolume` | The machine preset's `printable_area` and `printable_height`, following `inherits` |
115	| `nozzles` | The model file's `nozzle_diameter` |
116	| `assumed.nozzle` | The nozzle the model passed; else 0.4 when the model ships it; else its first size |
117	| `assumed.plate` | The model file's `default_bed_type`. **`null` when absent**, which is most printers (34 of 359 model files have one) |
118	| `assumed.filament` | The machine preset's `default_filament_profile` for that nozzle size, following `inherits`. This is OrcaSlicer's own default. Not the first entry of `default_materials`, which is the wizard's pre-ticked list (see 7) |
119	| `alreadyYours` | Whether a saved printer is this model |
120	
121	JSON, not prose, because `null` tells the model there is nothing to say (prose leaves a gap the model fills), values are quotable exactly, and the result can be checked and tested like every other tool in the app.
122	
123	### 5.5 Errors
124	
125	| Code | When | Message |
126	| --- | --- | --- |
127	| `unknown_printer` | An id is not on the list | Names the id; "copy it exactly from the printer list" |
128	| `too_many` | More than three ids | "More than three fit. Ask one question that narrows it down instead." |
129	| `unknown_nozzle` | The nozzle isn't one the model ships | Lists the sizes it ships |
130	
131	### 5.6 Approval
132	
133	None. The tool saves nothing; the person's tap on "Add this printer" is the decision.
134	
135	### 5.7 Worked examples (acceptance cases)
136	
137	**"the small bambu one"**
138	1. The model, from the list and its knowledge, settles on the A1 mini, and calls `{"catalogIds": ["BBL/N1"]}`.
139	2. The result gives the A1 mini: 180 × 180 × 180 mm; nozzles 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8; assumed 0.4 mm, Textured PEI Plate, Bambu PLA Basic @BBL A1M.
140	3. The model replies from those facts: "That's the Bambu Lab A1 mini. I'll assume the 0.4 mm nozzle, the Textured PEI plate and Bambu PLA Basic — change any of them here or in your first project."
141	
142	**"voron 2.4 350mm"**
143	The model reads "350mm" as the 350 size and calls `{"catalogIds": ["Voron/Voron2_350"]}`. The result has `"plate": null`, so the reply says nothing about a plate. No word matching happens anywhere.
144	
145	**"ender 3"**
146	Twelve models begin "Ender-3". The model does not call the tool; it asks which one and says the version is on the front label, or offers "Browse the list".
147	
148	**"the prusa, the 0.3 nozzle"**
149	The model calls `{"catalogIds": ["Prusa/MK3S"], "nozzle": 0.3}`, gets `unknown_nozzle` listing 0.25, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8, and asks which one it is.
150	
151	**"my elegoo mars"**
152	Not a filament printer. The model says so in one sentence; no tool call.
153	
154	## 6. `printer_change`
155	
156	### 6.1 Instructions (rules)
157	
158	- Work out what physically changed from what the person says; change only that.
159	- The plate belongs to each project, not the printer: say where to change it; no tool call.
160	- Nozzle material isn't tracked: say so; no tool call.
161	- Connecting a printer isn't possible from this panel: say so in one sentence.
162	- Report only what the tool's result says changed.
163	
164	### 6.2 Description (verbatim)
165	
166	> You work out what changed on this printer from what the person says. This tool checks it against what this printer's profile allows, asks the person to confirm, saves it, and returns the printer as it now is. It never decides what changed.
167	
168	### 6.3 Input
169	
170	```json
171	{ "nozzle": 0.6,                     // optional, mm
172	  "spools": [                        // optional; the complete list as it is now
173	    { "name": "Teal PLA", "material": "PLA", "colour": "#2a9d8f" } ] }
174	```
175	
176	At least one field. `spools` replaces the whole list; the model can restate it because its instructions carry the current list. No access code, no plate.
177	
178	### 6.4 Confirmation (Kenneth, 2026-09-18)
179	
180	- **Every call from the model shows a card** before anything is saved, stating the change in words:
181	
182	  ```
183	  Change nozzle
184	  0.4 mm → 0.6 mm on Bambu Lab A1 mini
185	  Every project that uses this printer slices for 0.6 mm.
186	                                Keep 0.4 mm   [Set 0.6 mm]
187	  ```
188	
189	  For spools, the card lists them before and after. No tool name on the card. The model is interpreting loose words ("i put a 0.6 on it", "I'm thinking of a 0.6"), and the change affects every project on that printer; the card is where a misreading is caught.
190	- **Undo is the app's, not the model's.** After a change the app adds "Nozzle set to 0.6 mm · Undo". Undo names the exact change, so it applies directly, through the same backend operation, without a card and without the model.
191	
192	### 6.5 Output (JSON)
193	
194	```json
195	{ "state": "applied",                // or "declined" when the person taps "Keep 0.4 mm"
196	  "changed": [ { "field": "nozzle", "before": 0.4, "after": 0.6 } ],
197	  "printer": { "name": "Bambu Lab A1 mini", "nozzle": 0.6, "nozzles": [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8],
198	               "spools": [ ], "connected": false } }
199	```
200	
201	The model states only what `changed` says happened, then may add its own advice ("with 0.6 you can print thicker layers"). On `declined` it says nothing changed.
202	
203	### 6.6 Errors
204	
205	| Code | When | Message |
206	| --- | --- | --- |
207	| `nothing_to_change` | No field given | "Name the nozzle or the spools that changed." |
208	| `unknown_nozzle` | The size isn't one the model ships | Lists the sizes it ships |
209	| `printer_gone` | The printer was renamed or removed while the card waited | Names the printer |
210	
211	### 6.7 Worked examples (acceptance cases)
212	
213	**"i put a 0.6 nozzle on it"** (A1 mini) → `{"nozzle": 0.6}` → card → "Set 0.6 mm" → `applied`, changed 0.4 → 0.6 → "Done — it's on the 0.6 mm nozzle now. You can print thicker layers with it."
214	
215	**"swapped to a hardened steel 0.4"** → no call: "The size is still 0.4 mm, so nothing changes here; the app doesn't track nozzle material."
216	
217	**"the plate is smooth PEI now"** → no call: the plate is chosen per project, in the project's printer menu.
218	
219	**"i put a 0.3 on it"** → `{"nozzle": 0.3}` → `unknown_nozzle` listing 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 → the model asks which it is.
220	
221	## 7. What the app tells the model: events
222	
223	The app records its own actions as **events**: one plain sentence each, stating what happened (examples in section 3). Rules:
224	
225	- **Statements, never instructions.** "The person chose Prusa MK3S", never "Propose Prusa MK3S".
226	- **Events reach the model.** Today the only way the app writes to the thread is a note (`AgentHost::post_note`), and notes are deliberately left out of the model's context (`J/Agent/AgentHost.cpp`, around line 1608: "Notes stay out of the model's context"). That rule exists because in the project conversation a note restates project state the model already receives in full, and a stale note could contradict it. A printer conversation receives no project state, so the reason does not apply there. **Decided: in the printer conversation, notes are included in the model's context**, in order, as app statements (not as the person's words and not as the model's own). The project conversation keeps excluding them. Record events as notes. Test both: a printer conversation's next request carries its notes; a project conversation's does not.
227	- **Most events start no model turn.** Only "Not this one", and a network printer the app cannot match, start one, because only then does the person need the model's next words.
228	- **Events count toward the history limit.** The model is given the last 20 messages today (`kHistoryMessages`). Events are part of the conversation, so they count like any other message; an Add or Change conversation rarely approaches 20.
229	
230	## 8. What to remove from `0e55c4f9be`
231	
232	- `printer_catalog_search`, `printer_propose`, `printer_suggest` from the registry (`J/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`, around line 1432), and `OrcaPrinterBackend::search_catalog`.
233	- Every `ask_agent` prompt that tells the model what to call (`J/PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp`).
234	- Scripted button labels in the instructions.
235	- The `planId` field the registry adds to every change tool (`joins_plans`, `J/Agent/ToolRegistry.hpp`): neither printer tool joins grouped approvals.
236	- The project workspace in printer tool results.
237	- `accessCode` from `printer_change`, and the "access code, optional" placeholder that asks for it in the chat.
238	- `say`, `question`, `action`, `reason`, `plate`, `filament` and `provenance` inputs from any identify tool.
239	
240	## 9. Back-end fixes this design depends on
241	
242	- **Per-session tool lists by mode:** Add offers only `printer_identify`, Change only `printer_change`. Offering every tool in both modes lets a Change conversation call the identify tool and clear the pinned card of an existing printer.
243	- **Default filament from the right field.** `PrinterCatalog.cpp` (around line 143) takes the first entry of `default_materials` and falls back to `default_filament_profile` only when that list is empty. For the Prusa MK3S that yields "Prusa Generic ABS". Read `default_filament_profile` for the chosen nozzle, and save and show that same value.
244	- **Plate unknown is `null`,** never a guess.
245	- **A nozzle change must not touch the open project.** `Printers::change_named_printer_nozzle` selects the printer in the plater before saving and can raise OrcaSlicer's unsaved-changes dialog (`J/Printers/NamedPrinters.cpp`, around line 333; read, not run). Changing a printer from Home must leave the project's printer selection and modified flag alone.
246	- **Events in the model's context** (section 7).
247	
248	## 10. Verification
249	
250	- **Re-measure identification on the model the app ships.** The spikes measured `gpt-5.6-terra` answering in JSON. The app is pinned to `gpt-5.4-mini` (`J/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.hpp:58`) and answers through a tool call. Run both spike test sets (`agent-docs/jusprin/spikes/printer-naming/corpus.jsonl` and `spikes/printer-photos/corpus.jsonl`, present but uncommitted in the `claude/printer-conversation-panel-af11cb` worktree) through the real tool path on `gpt-5.4-mini`, plus the cases that failed in testing: "x1c", "voron 2.4 350mm", "prusa", "ender 3".
251	- **The worked examples in 5.7 and 6.7 pass** in the built app with the live agent.
252	- **Unit tests:**
253	  - each tool's input checks (id counts, unknown ids, nozzle sizes);
254	  - results carry no workspace;
255	  - each mode offers only its own tool;
256	  - no event is an instruction, and events reach the model's context;
257	  - no access code enters a tool input or the conversation;
258	  - a nozzle change leaves the open project's selection and modified flag untouched;
259	  - Undo applies without a card.
260	- **Measure the footprint** as the tool guide requires (`agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md`): definition bytes per mode, and input and cached tokens per request, for an Add and a Change conversation.
261	- **Update the tool guide:** the printer session's per-mode tool list; the whole-list-in-the-prompt exception to "use bounded search", with the spike as evidence; both tools in the catalog record.
262	
263	## 11. Decisions (Kenneth)
264	
265	- 2026-09-17: the real in-app agent handles adding and changing printers; the Orca Arena bundle is hidden from the add-printer flow only (still in the wizard); no agent set up means the agent-setup page.
266	- 2026-09-18: two tools, one per mode, as specified here; a change the model works out from typed words always shows the confirmation card; Undo applies directly.
267	
268	## 12. Open questions
269	
270	- None known. If implementing reveals a conflict between this document and the code or wireframes, stop and ask Kenneth rather than choosing.

The doc (section 5.1) gave the model seven rules for working out which printer someone has:

1. If one printer fits, show it.
2. If two or three fit, show them all and ask what tells them apart.
3. If more than three fit, don't show any. Ask one narrowing question, or point to the full list.
4. If what the person typed is the start of several model names, it isn't a clear match, even if it's exactly one of those names. For example, "ender 3" is a model, but it's also the start of Ender-3 Pro, Ender-3 V2 and nine others.
5. If nothing fits, or it's a resin or laser machine, say so in one sentence.
6. For photos, only name a model from a readable label or printed size, and ask for a photo of the label otherwise.
7. Write replies only from what the tool returns, never from memory.

 Did you set these rules? If so, are you trying to overwrite, are you trying to use static stupid rules to overwrite llm intelligence?

Yes, I wrote them. Most came from the earlier test prompt; I added rule 3, the "one sentence" in rule 5, and rule 7. I didn't intend to override the model, but several of them do: they replace its judgment with a fixed answer instead of telling it what it can't know and letting it decide.

The test for each rule: is it something the model can't know about the app (fine to tell it), or a decision it could make itself (it shouldn't be a rule)?

1. **One fits → show it.** Mostly fine: the model needs to know that one printer gets an "Add" button. Say that, not "show it".
2. **Two or three → show them and ask.** The same kind of fact: the panel shows up to three cards to choose from. Whether to ask, and what to ask, is the model's call.
3. **More than three → show none.** That overrides it. The model can't know two things: the panel fits at most three cards, and showing three of twelve makes people think that's all of them. Tell it those, and it can decide — say, show the two most likely and name the rest.
4. **"ender 3" isn't a clear match.** A patch for one mistake, made by a different model in testing, turned into a blanket rule. It's wrong when someone owns the original Ender-3. The only fact behind it: people often type a shortened name.
5. **Nothing fits → say so in one sentence.** "Say so" is fine, since there's nothing to show. "One sentence" is micromanaging.
6. **Photos: only name a model from a readable label.** The reason behind it is real. In testing, guesses by shape alone were wrong about half the time, and a wrong printer means wrong slicing. But as a blanket ban it overrides the model even when a machine is unmistakable. Give it the fact and the cost, and let it weigh them.
7. **Only from what the tool returns, never from memory.** Far too broad: it would stop the model answering "can it print PETG?" The only valid part: the nozzle, plate and filament the app will actually use come from the tool's result, so state those from the result.

What should stay as fixed rules are the app's real limits: at most three printers per call, only printers from the list, and no call when nothing fits.

I'd rewrite section 5.1 that way — the app's facts plus those three limits — and apply the same test to the change rules in 6.1. Want me to do it?

Based on the search results, here's what Anthropic recommends about adding context and explaining the motivation behind instructions:

## Adding Context and Explaining Why

Providing context or motivation behind your instructions, such as explaining to Claude why such behavior is important, can help Claude better understand your goals and deliver more targeted responses.

## Why This Matters

Prompt engineering is ultimately about communication: speaking the language that helps AI most clearly understand your intent. The difference between a vague instruction and a well-crafted prompt can mean the gap between generic outputs and exactly what you need. A poorly structured prompt might require multiple back-and-forth exchanges to clarify intent, while a well-engineered prompt gets you there in one shot.

## Practical Application

Provide context about what the output is for, who the audience is, and what success looks like. Additionally, provide context for your constraints (for example, 'never use ellipses because this will be read by text-to-speech').

The broader principle is that LLMs are constrained by a finite attention budget, so good context engineering means finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome. This means being intentional about which context and explanations add real value to your instructions.

# System Prompts at the Right Altitude

The article describes two failure modes when calibrating system prompts:

**Overly complex approach:** "engineers hardcoding complex, brittle logic in their prompts to elicit exact agentic behavior. This approach creates fragility and increases maintenance complexity over time."

**Overly vague approach:** Engineers sometimes offer "vague, high-level guidance that fails to give the LLM concrete signals for desired outputs or falsely assumes shared context."

**The balanced solution:** The optimal approach strikes a middle ground—"specific enough to guide behavior effectively, yet flexible enough to provide the model with strong heuristics to guide behavior."

The key principle is finding the Goldilocks zone: sufficiently detailed to direct the model's actions without becoming rigid or fragile, yet general enough to allow the model reasoning flexibility.

content.text:
The better option is context and constraints: tell the model what we're trying to achieve and what the app can and can't do, then let it decide. Anthropic's published guidance says this directly, and my rules were the failure mode it warns against.

What the guidance says:
- **Explain why, don't just command.** Giving the reason behind an instruction helps the model understand the goal. Its example: rather than "never use ellipses", say that the response will be read aloud by text-to-speech, which can't pronounce them ([Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)).
- **Two ways to get it wrong.** Anthropic's article on building agent prompts names "engineers hardcoding complex, brittle logic in their prompts to elicit exact agentic behavior", which "creates fragility". The opposite failure is vague guidance that assumes shared context. The target in between is prompts "specific enough to guide behavior effectively, yet flexible enough to provide the model with strong heuristics" ([Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)).

Rules 3, 4 and 7 are that brittle kind. Rule 4 is a patch for one mistake one model made, written as an absolute.

So, instead of the seven rules, the model should get:
1. **The goal.** Get the person's exact printer right, because a wrong printer means every print is sliced wrong. Make it quick for someone who may not know their model's exact name.
2. **What the app does with its answer.** One printer gets an "Add" button; two or three become cards to pick from; the panel can't show more than three; showing a few of many makes people think that's all of them; the list is complete; the tool returns what the app will assume (nozzle, plate, filament).
3. **What's known to go wrong.** People often type shortened names. In testing, guessing a printer from its shape in a photo was wrong about half the time, while a readable label was almost always right.
4. **Hard limits, enforced by the tool rather than just asked for in the prompt.** At most three printers, only printers from the list. If the model breaks one, the tool's error explains it.

Two caveats:
- **The guidance I cited is Anthropic's.** The app runs an OpenAI model (`gpt-5.4-mini`), and I haven't checked OpenAI's own prompting guide.
- **The rule version has evidence behind it.** In the earlier test, adding rule 4 took one model from 47 to 50 correct out of 50. The honest way to settle it is to run the same test cases on `gpt-5.4-mini` with both versions — the context-and-constraints prompt against the rule list — and keep whichever gets more right. I'd expect the context version to match or beat the rules, but that's a prediction, not something I've measured.
